1. **The idea.** The frames show a grid of squares, one per starting period in US history. Each square is "lit" (light cream) if a buyer was ahead after ten years, or dark brown if the renter who invested the difference had the bigger pile. The point is that neither side wins every time. The result depends on when you start.

2. **What changes.** The grid itself stays mostly the same. Text labels and a highlighted band are added as the frames go on. Frame 1 has only the label "after the crash: lit again". From frame 2, a caption reads "2009 to mid-2016: nearly 4 in 5 lit", and a pale band marks that stretch of the grid. From frame 3, a second label reads "lit in stretches · one long dark stretch", pointing to the large dark block in the middle. By frame 6 all three labels are showing and the band is gone.

3. **What it means.** Buying came out ahead in some periods and renting-and-investing in others. Buyers did well in clusters of years, such as starts after the housing crash. Renters won in one long continuous stretch. So "rent and invest the difference" does not always win, and neither does buying. Which one came out ahead depended on the start date. The footer says "US only · history, not a forecast", and the "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag suggests the grid is a schematic and not exact data.

4. **Advice a viewer would take.** The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer would probably conclude that the outcome depends on timing and that neither choice is guaranteed to come out ahead. Past results don't predict future ones.

5. **Source of the conclusion.** The animation supports the "it depends on timing" reading directly, through "lit in stretches · one long dark stretch" and "history, not a forecast". It does not tell the viewer what to do. Any advice beyond "outcomes vary by start period and past results aren't a forecast" would be my own conclusion.
